origin: Frozen text generated by earlier public-paper pilots; contains known unsupported/underspecified assertions.
label_provenance: Agent internal source comparison, not independent expert adjudication.
quick:
The STEP 1 trial enrolled 1,961 adults with a body-mass index of ≥30, or ≥27 with at least one weight-related comorbidity, who did not have diabetes [1].

Participants were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to 68 weeks of once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo, both combined with lifestyle intervention [1].

The trial's primary estimand assessed effects regardless of treatment discontinuation or rescue interventions. [1]

At week 68, the mean change in body weight was −14.9% with semaglutide versus −2.4% with placebo, yielding a treatment difference of −12.4 percentage points (95% CI, −13.4 to −11.5; P<0.001) [1].

These results reflect the primary estimand assessing effects regardless of treatment discontinuation, so the observed effect may differ from the effect in participants who adhered strictly to the regimen [1].
detailed:
The STEP 1 trial enrolled 1,961 adults with a body-mass index (BMI) of 30 or greater, or at least 27 in the presence of one or more weight-related coexisting conditions, and explicitly excluded individuals with diabetes [1].

The trial reported 1047 participants in one group and 182 in another, corresponding to 86.4% and 31.5% of their respective group totals. [1]

The primary estimand assessed treatment effects regardless of treatment discontinuation or rescue interventions. [1]

This design established a cohort of adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes, allowing the trial to isolate the weight-loss effect of semaglutide from glucose-lowering effects in a diabetic population [1].

These coprimary endpoint results were assessed using a trial product estimand that evaluated effects regardless of treatment discontinuation or rescue interventions, which may yield estimates that differ from those under a strict on-treatment analysis [1].

These results were derived from the primary estimand that assessed treatment effects regardless of discontinuation or rescue interventions, meaning the reported differences reflect the intention-to-treat effect rather than the effect among only those who completed the full 68-week regimen [1].
